t.1.146.1: You should never give way to grief like an ordinary man; for you, a man of learning, this is no time for grief.
t.1.146.2: Death must inevitably be reached here by all men; over a matter that is bound to come to pass, there is surely no cause for grief here.
t.1.146.3: A wife, a son, and a daughter: all are desired for one's own sake. Cast off your anguish with clear understanding; I myself shall go there.
t.1.146.4: For this is the highest and eternal duty of a woman in the world: that, even giving up her very life, she should do what is good for her husband.
t.1.146.5: And that deed, done there, brings happiness to you here as well; it becomes imperishable in the world beyond and brings glory in this world.
t.1.146.7: The purpose for which a wife is desired, that purpose you have attained in me: a daughter and a son as well; by you I have been made free of debt.
t.1.146.6: And this is the weighty duty that I shall declare to you; in it both your advantage and your dharma are seen to be the greater.
t.1.146.8: You are capable of nourishing and likewise of protecting our two children, but I am not able in the same way to protect and nourish the two children.
t.1.146.9: For to me, bereft of you, all our desires would turn into calamities. How would our two young children fare, and how indeed would I?
t.1.146.10: For how, without you, shall I, a widow without a protector and with young children, keep this pair alive while still keeping to the path the virtuous have walked?
t.1.146.12: Just as birds covet a piece of meat dropped upon the ground, so all men covet a woman who is bereft of her husband.
t.1.146.11: How shall I, a proud woman, be able to protect this daughter when she is sought after by haughty men who are unfit for alliance with you?
t.1.146.13: Shaken and solicited by wicked men, I shall not be able to keep to the path cherished by the virtuous, O best of the twice-born.
t.1.146.14: How can I bring myself to send this young girl, the only one of your family, still unmarried, down the path our fathers and grandfathers have taken?
t.1.146.15: How shall I be able to instill the desired virtues in this boy, helpless and bereft on every side, as you, who have seen dharma, would have done?
t.1.146.16: And unworthy men, scorning me, will seek after this young daughter of yours, left without a protector, just as śūdras covet the hearing of the Veda.
t.1.146.17: If I were unwilling to give her away, enriched as she is by your virtues, they would carry her off by force, as crows snatch the oblation from the sacrifice.
t.1.146.20: Those two young sons of mine, bereft of me and of you as well, would surely perish, there is no doubt, like two fish when the water dries up.
t.1.146.19: Despised by the world and by arrogant men, and not knowing how to look after myself, I shall die, O brahmin; of that there is no doubt.
t.1.146.18: Beholding your son as though in a state unworthy of himself, and this daughter of yours too, fallen into the power of the unworthy…
t.1.146.21: In every way, then, this group of three, bereft of you, will without doubt perish; therefore you ought to give me up.
t.1.146.23: For your sake I have given up this son and likewise this daughter; I have given up my kinsmen, and my very life as well.
t.1.146.22: This is the highest blessing for women: to go before their husband to the supreme goal, and not, O brāhmaṇa, to live on in the domain of their sons.
t.1.146.24: A wife's constant steadfastness in what is pleasing and beneficial to her husband surpasses sacrifices, austerities, observances and the various kinds of gifts.
t.1.146.25: This, then, which I wish to do is righteous and highly approved, both desirable and beneficial, for you as well as for the family.
t.1.146.26: Children, wealth, dear friends, and a wife as well are desired for deliverance from the trials of misfortune; such is the view of the virtuous.
t.1.146.27: On one side the entire family, on the other one's own self, O increaser of the family: the two are not at all equal. This is the firm conclusion of the wise.
t.1.146.29: Those who know the law say that in deciding what is right, women are not to be slain; and they say the Rākṣasas know the law, so he would not kill me either.
t.1.146.28: So accomplish through me what must be done, and save yourself by your own self; give me leave, noble one, and protect my two sons.
t.1.146.30: For men, death is beyond doubt; for women, death is a matter of doubt. Therefore, O knower of dharma, you should send me alone.
t.1.146.32: I have borne a son, I am old, and I have always sought what is dear to you; having considered all this, I am making this resolve.
t.1.146.31: I have enjoyed life, I have obtained what was dear to me, and I have practised dharma; I have gained beloved offspring through you, so the loss of my life will not grieve me.
t.1.146.34: And it is no unrighteousness, good man, for men to have many wives; but for women it is a very great unrighteousness to transgress against a former husband.
t.1.146.33: Even after giving me up, noble one, you will find another woman, and then your dharma will once again be firmly established.
t.1.146.35: Having considered all this, and that the sacrifice of oneself is condemned, save yourself through me, and save the family and these two children.
t.1.146.36: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by her, the husband embraced her, O Bhārata, and, deeply grieved, he slowly shed tears together with his wife.
